_meta.description: Rules for deriving graph edges from findings. Content, not code: adding an edge kind is a data change, exactly as adding an attack path is.
_meta.what_an_edge_claims: That two objects named by ONE finding stand in the stated relationship, because the check that produced the finding is about that relationship. Nothing here is traversed, reached or validated: every edge is written with confidence 'derived_from_config' and the console repeats it.
_meta.what_an_edge_never_claims: That THIS relationship was exercised. An edge from a user carries provenance 'used' when the logon export shows that user logging on successfully in the window, which evidences that the ACCOUNT is live — not that it invoked this role or destination, which no configuration export could show. Without a logon export every edge is 'configured', recording that nobody looked at activity rather than that nothing is active.
_meta.the_pairing_rule: A finding lists its objects FLAT. AUTH-002 names one role, one authorization object and two users, and which user holds which role is visible only in the display string. So an edge is emitted ONLY where the pairing is unambiguous — one side names exactly one object of its type — and where both sides are plural the finding is declined and counted. Reading the pairing out of affected_items would resurrect the 'display' basis this product retired.
_meta.how_a_module_escapes_the_pairing_rule: By declaring it. A finding may carry `relations` — explicit {from, to} pairs — and where it does, those pairs are used as evidence and the ambiguity question never arises. Measured before this existed: 42 of the 76 findings naming two object types named both sides plural and were declined, which is most of the reason a 939-node graph held 15 edges. The pairing was usually not unknown to the module, only unrepresentable: check_critical_profiles built a list it called `object_pairs` and flattened it one line later. A module still says only WHICH objects relate; what the relationship is called stays here, so declaring relations cannot invent edge vocabulary.
_meta.why_not_the_transitive_edge: AUTH-002 evidences user->role and role->auth_object. It does NOT evidence a user->auth_object edge: that is the transitive closure, and asserting it as an edge would state as observed what is only implied.
sources: server/schema.sql — graph_edge, whose provenance/confidence/owner columns this fills
server/identity.py — extract_nodes, whose typed objects these edges join

rules.why: USR-002 reports users holding SAP_ALL, SAP_NEW or S_A.SYSTEM, and the assignment IS the finding. A profile is not a role — in SAP a role generates a profile and the two are separate objects — so this is its own edge type rather than a second spelling of holds_role. The check declares the pairing in `relations`, so which user holds which profile is evidence here rather than inference.

An armed background job executes its steps with the step user's authorisations (TBTCP-AUTHCKNAM). `check_job_privileged_step_user` already said what this is for: 'the job->user edge is what makes "this armed job runs as DDIC" derivable'. The direction is the job's, not the user's — the job borrows the identity, the user does not reach for the job — so this is NOT an actor edge and `path_actors` does not walk it.

An armed job step names the ABAP program it executes (TBTCP-PROGNAME), and RSBDCOS0 in that position is the OS bridge that bypasses the SM69 allowlist entirely. Emitted as a second edge FROM THE JOB rather than as the chain the check's own comment sketches: 'job -> program -> user' reads as though the program runs as the step user, and nothing in the export says that — the job runs the program and the job runs as the user.

The scheduler named in SDLUNAME arranged for the job to run. Kept separate from runs_as deliberately: together the two edges say a lower-privileged scheduler gets code executed under a stronger identity, which is exactly what the check reports — but as two facts a reader joins, never as a scheduler->step-user edge. That edge would read as 'this account can act as that one', a conclusion rather than something the export states, and the same transitive claim why_not_the_transitive_edge already refuses.

A super-admin business-role template assigned to a business user is the same relationship the AUTH- and IAM-EXP- rules describe, reached through the S/4HANA business-role export rather than PFCG. Same edge type deliberately: SAP_BR_ADMINISTRATOR held by a user is a role assignment, and giving it a second name would split one relationship across two vocabularies.

A BTP role collection granted to a subaccount user is the platform's own privilege assignment, and this check exists to report the administrative ones. Not holds_role: a role collection is a BTP object with case-sensitive naming, and conflating it with a PFCG role would merge two different objects that can share a spelling — the same reason the check types them separately.

A HANA system privilege granted to a database user is the database half of the same relationship holds_profile describes on the ABAP side, and the checks in this family exist to report exactly that grant. `check_system_privileges` already carried the comment 'a grant is an edge: both ends become graph nodes' — both ends did, and which end went with which did not, so the database estate contributed no privilege edges at all until the pairing could be declared.

The same relationship one level up: a predefined HANA role granted to a database user. Separate from holds_hana_privilege because a role and a privilege are separate objects in HANA, and one edge type spanning both would lose which of the two was actually granted.
The AUTH-* family reports role content and attributes it to the users who hold the role. The assignment is the relationship the check is about.
The same findings name the authorization object whose values made the role risky. A role granting S_RFCACL is the edge that matters, not the user who happens to hold it.
AUTH-013 is about transaction access carried by a role, so the role->tcode relationship is the finding's own subject.
The privilege-escalation checks name the user and the role that grants the escalation. Same relationship as the AUTH- family, different evidence.
A trusted destination usable by a named user is the relationship the check exists to report — it is the hop a caller would take between systems.
